# Identifying changes in viral fitness using population genetic structure

**Authors:** Brittany A Petros

**Affiliations:** aGenomic Center for Infectious Diseases, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA 02142 | bHealth Sciences and Technology, Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139 | cHarvard/MIT MD-PhD Program, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115 | dDepartment of Systems Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115

Viruses, particularly RNA viruses, evolve rapidly due to their high mutation rates and short generation times (1). Viruses possessing beneficial mutations—for example, mutations that increase viral transmissibility (2) or evade vaccine-induced immunity (3)—have more opportunities to replicate and thus constitute an increasing fraction of the viral population. The relative growth rate of a viral mutant can therefore serve as a proxy for the fitness of the mutant, relative to the fitness of the rest of the viral population (4, 5). In this issue of PNAS, Donker et al. develop a new method to identify changes in the fitness of SARS-CoV-2 and the mutants responsible for these changes (6).

It is important to rapidly identify viral mutants with increased fitness, as these mutants may increase the burden of viral disease (7) or reduce the efficacy of prophylactic or therapeutic measures (8). In a process termed genomic surveillance, scientists and public health officials generate and analyze viral genetic sequences. Contemporary and contextual viral sequences can be used to construct phylogenetic trees, which are graphical depictions of the inferred evolutionary relationships between various viral mutants. When a particular group of evolutionarily related viral mutants is deemed epidemiologically important—for example, because this group of mutants is increasing in abundance—the group is given a taxonomic classification as a particular viral variant (e.g., the Omicron variant). This nomenclature serves as a useful way to refer to a collection of related viral mutants in epidemiologic and evolutionary studies, including those that aim to estimate viral fitness.

However, there are multiple challenges associated with using a phylogenetic approach to identify important viral variants. First, inferring phylogenetic trees from viral genetic sequences is a computationally demanding task, particularly when using tens of thousands of sequences (9). Additionally, the division of viral mutants into specific taxonomic categories (i.e., viral variants) is somewhat arbitrary, with divisions that are too coarse or too fine failing to adequately capture groups of mutants that share ecological or phenotypic properties (10). To circumvent this issue, viral variant classification tools have focused on defining new groupings only for viral mutants that have already demonstrated epidemiologic importance (11, 12). This workaround results in reactive approaches to public health, in which a variant is named only after significant viral spread has already occurred (13).

In PNAS, Donker et al. develop a new method to identify changes in the fitness of SARS-CoV-2 and the mutants responsible for these changes.

To address these shortcomings, Donker et al. develop a mathematical method to rapidly identify increases in the fitness of SARS-CoV-2 as well as the responsible viral mutants. Their approach is highly scalable, taking under 90 s to perform on nearly 3 million viral sequences, and accurately identifies the increases in viral fitness associated with the emergence of the Alpha, Delta, and Omicron variants. In contrast to the previously described approaches, this method makes inferences directly from the viral sequences without relying on viral variant classification tools or phylogenetic trees. Moreover, this approach has the potential to identify increases in viral fitness in advance of increases in incident cases, suggesting that this method could inform proactive public health responses.

How does their method work? Donker et al. use a modified form of the fixation index, FST, which is a commonly used statistic in population biology (14). This index measures the degree to which two subpopulations differ genetically. Classically, the population is divided into subpopulations based on geographic boundaries (e.g., the domestic cats in the United States and the domestic cats in Europe) (15). The key insight is that the SARS-CoV-2 sequences collected at a given time t can be considered a subpopulation. Donker et al. then calculate the modified form of the fixation index to measure the degree to which the viral population at time t is genetically distinct from the viral population at time t + T, where T is a constant amount of time. For example, the Delta variant circulated for multiple months during which the FST was relatively constant over successive time intervals. However, the emergence of the Omicron variant was associated with a change in the population genetic structure and was reflected in an increase in FST. Donker et al. use this increase in FST as a marker of increased viral fitness, with the change in the slope of the graph of FST over time serving as a quantitative metric of the emerging viral variant’s relative fitness advantage (Fig. 1).

*Fig. 1.: Schematic depiction of the mathematical approach developed by Donker et al. SARS-CoV-2 genetic sequences from samples isolated over a particular time interval (e.g., 1 wk) are grouped with one another. These sequences are considered one subpopulation and are compared to sequences isolated over the previous time interval (e.g., last week’s subpopulation) and to sequences isolated over the following time interval (e.g., next week’s subpopulation). To quantify the genetic divergence of the viral population over time, a modified form of the fixation index, FST, is calculated for each pair of successive subpopulations. Changes in the slope of the fixation index over time provide a quantitative metric of the relative growth rate (i.e., a proxy for the relative fitness advantage) of the viral mutants spreading in the population.*

There are several attractive features of this approach. Unlike phylogenetic methods, it is scalable, with the per-sample computation time decreasing as the number of input viral sequences increases. This method is also relatively robust to sequencing errors and inconsistencies in the bioinformatic pipelines used to generate pathogen genomes, as it relies on relative, rather than absolute, measures of genetic diversity. Moreover, their approach can be easily adapted to accommodate viral sequences derived from environmental sampling (16–18) because rapidly growing viral variants will still have the expected effect on the fixation index of subpopulations of sequences derived from serially collected pooled samples.

The primary limitation of this approach is not methodological but instead concerns the availability of input data that accurately represents circulating viral variation. Donker et al. demonstrate that their approach is reliable when using as few as 100 SARS-CoV-2 sequences per week per geographic area (e.g., country). However, no other viral pathogens are regularly sequenced at this cadence, and SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance efforts fall short of producing 100 genomes weekly in many countries (19). Delays in the time between the isolation of SARS-CoV-2-positive samples and the submission of viral genomes to public databases can also reduce the real-time public health utility of the tool (20). Underlying both of these issues is the need to address the many barriers that hinder globally representative, real-time pathogen genomic surveillance (21). Moreover, while an increase in the presence of a viral variant in genomic databases is a reasonable proxy for viral fitness, it is an imperfect proxy. For example, the implementation or discontinuation of various nonpharmaceutical interventions can alter a variant’s derived growth rate without impacting its intrinsic fitness. Genomic surveillance approaches that are biased toward particular viral variants—such as the preferential sequencing of samples with S-gene target failure (22)—will also artificially change the derived fitness of viral variants. Additional parameters that account for changes in public health interventions or sampling strategies (23) can be incorporated into this tool to address these biases. Combined with continued investment in improving genomic surveillance, the authors’ approach holds promise in bringing genetically informed insights into public health responses.
